exchanges.speaker: Pilot
exchanges.text: Hong Kong Radar, Cathay two five one, passing eight thousand feet climbing to Flight Level one six zero.
exchanges.meaning: Initial climb check-in: station, callsign, passing altitude and cleared level.

exchanges.speaker: ATC
exchanges.text: Cathay two five one, Hong Kong Radar, climb to Flight Level one six zero, transition altitude nine thousand, standard altimeter setting one zero one three.
exchanges.meaning: ATC clears the climb to FL160 and issues the transition altitude with the standard pressure setting.

exchanges.speaker: Pilot
exchanges.text: Climb to Flight Level one six zero, standard set one zero one three, Cathay two five one.
exchanges.meaning: Pilot reads back the cleared level and the standard altimeter setting.

exchanges.speaker: ATC
exchanges.text: Cathay two five one, stop climb at Flight Level one four zero, expedite climb through Flight Level one wun zero, traffic twelve o'clock opposite direction Boeing seven seven seven level at Flight Level one fife zero.
exchanges.meaning: Urgent instruction: stop the climb at FL140 but expedite through FL110 due to opposite-direction traffic at FL150.

exchanges.speaker: Pilot
exchanges.text: Stopping climb at Flight Level one four zero, expediting climb through Flight Level one wun zero, traffic in sight, Cathay two five one.
exchanges.meaning: Pilot confirms stopping the climb at FL140, expediting through FL110, with the traffic in sight.

exchanges.speaker: Pilot
exchanges.text: Stopping climb at Flight Level one four zero, standard altimeter one zero one three, Cathay two five one.
exchanges.meaning: Correct readback form: the standard keyword is 'stopping climb' (never 'level off'), and the pressure value must be read back numerically.

vocabulary.definition: 9,000 ft at Hong Kong (VHHH). Below this, fly on QNH (altitudes).
Lowest usable flight level above the transition altitude (e.g. FL110), assigned by ATC.
1013.25 hPa / 29.92 inHg (QNE); the altimeter subscale used above the transition altitude.
Immediate ATC instruction to level off at the assigned flight level.
Climb at best rate (Vy) to clear a traffic conflict.
Climbing or descending through an assigned level without clearance.

quiz.question: An aircraft is cruising at 4,500 ft on a QNH of 1025 hPa. The aircraft enters an area where the actual sea level pressure is 1005 hPa, but the pilot forgets to adjust the altimeter subscale. What is the aircraft's true altitude relative to its indicated altitude?
quiz.explanation: 1 hPa is approximately 30 ft. A 20 hPa pressure drop equals approximately 600 ft. Flying from high to low pressure without resetting the subscale causes the altimeter to overread, placing the aircraft 600 ft lower than indicated.

quiz.question: Under ICAO Doc 9432, what is the standardized instruction when ATC requires an aircraft to climb at the maximum operational rate to avoid traffic?
options: Climb as fast as possible to Flight Level...
Maximum vertical speed to Flight Level...
quiz.explanation: ICAO standardizes EXPEDITE (paired with climb or descent) to command maximum operational rate without exceeding aircraft aerodynamic limits.

sections.heading: Core Learning Content -- Level Bust Prevention & Altimetry
sections.body:
- Transition Altitude (TA): 9,000 ft at Hong Kong (VHHH). Below this, fly on QNH (altitudes).
- Transition Level (TL): Lowest usable flight level above TA (e.g. FL110), assigned by ATC.
- Standard Pressure Setting: 1013.25 hPa / 29.92 inHg (QNE).
- Stop Climb At [FL]: Immediate instruction to level off.
- Expedite Climb: Best rate of climb (Vy) to clear traffic conflicts.

sections.heading: Spaced Repetition Drill
sections.body:
- Day 12 Review (+1d): Cancelling SID altitude restrictions does NOT cancel lateral waypoints or published speed restrictions.
- Day 10 Review (+3d): In cold air, true altitude is lower than indicated altitude ("from warm to cold, look out below").

sections.heading: Fun Aviation Fact
sections.body: Transition Altitudes vary worldwide: 9,000 ft in Hong Kong, 18,000 ft in the USA/Canada, and 3,000-6,000 ft in the UK and Europe.
